summary: Builds on RFC 1006, which supplies the ISO transport service over TCP, to show how the OSI session, presentation, and application layers can be run on top of it. This lets OSI applications work on TCP/IP-based internets.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people speak different languages but share a phone line. This explains how to put the other group's speech rules on top of the phone line the Internet already has.

questions: iso presentation services over tcp ip
how to run osi applications on tcp ip
subtitle: Lightweight OSI application layer support over TCP/IP networks.

tldr.problem: Organizations want to run ISO OSI applications on TCP/IP networks, but implementing the full OSI stack (presentation, session, transport layers) is expensive.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a minimal presentation layer that serializes ASN.1 data objects directly over TCP or UDP, hard-wiring most parameters instead of negotiating them, and handling the essential connection management and data transfer functions.
tldr.outcome: Applications using only ACSE and ROSE service elements can run on TCP/IP with much less infrastructure than a full OSI implementation, though with reduced flexibility.

facts.label: Target applications
facts.value: OSI apps with ACSE and ROSE only

today: RFC 1085 is not an Internet Standard. It proposed a mechanism for running a subset of OSI applications on TCP/IP networks, particularly for CMIP-based management. As TCP/IP became dominant and management moved toward SNMP and later protocols, this approach saw limited deployment. The RFC remains available for implementations that need lightweight OSI application support, but is not widely used in modern networks.

sections.title: Why Run OSI Applications on TCP/IP
sections.content:
RFC 1006 showed how to run ISO transport services over TCP. This memo builds on that to run the OSI presentation, session, and application layers on top, letting OSI applications work in TCP/IP networks. The challenge is to do this in environments where implementing the full OSI stack is impractical, such as embedded systems or specialized management agents. The mechanism is streamlined and minimal.

The motivation came from a need to run ISO Common Management Information Protocol (CMIP) in TCP/IP networks with a lighter resource footprint than a full OSI implementation would require.
sections.plainLanguage: Some programs expect to use the OSI network rules. This explains how to let them run on the Internet without rewriting them completely.

sections.title: What Applications This Covers
sections.content: This mechanism is designed for OSI applications whose service elements consist of only ACSE (Association Control Service Element) and ROSE (Remote Operations Service Element), plus a minimal Directory Services Element. ACSE manages connections between application entities; ROSE orchestrates the invocation of operations. The mechanism provides the presentation layer services these need: connection establishment, data transfer, and connection termination. It does not support more complex OSI applications with additional service elements.
sections.plainLanguage: This is for programs that need to set up a conversation, ask for operations to be done, and close the conversation. More complicated programs would need a different approach.

sections.title: The Simplified Approach
sections.content:
The key insight is that ASN.1 objects (abstract data descriptions) are self-delimiting when serialized as octets, and TCP is a stream-oriented transport. Instead of negotiating presentation contexts and transfer syntaxes as the full ISO presentation protocol does, this RFC hard-wires essential parameters and sends ASN.1 objects directly over the TCP stream. The presentation provider consists of a dispatch module (offering the presentation interface), a serialization module (encoding/decoding ASN.1 using basic encoding rules), and a network module (managing the TCP connection). No presentation-layer negotiation occurs.

The RFC also permits using UDP as the underlying transport for a lower-quality service, though with added complexity because UDP is packet-oriented rather than stream-oriented.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of negotiating rules for every conversation, both sides agree to use the same rules from the start. Data gets packed into a standard format and sent straight through the pipe.

sections.title: Establishing and Ending Connections
sections.content: Connections are established using the P-CONNECT service, which creates a presentation connection with two fixed presentation contexts: one for ACSE and one for the application service. The quality of service parameter selects TCP (high reliability) or UDP (low reliability). The calling and called presentation addresses contain IP addresses, port numbers, and optional selectors. A presentation connection is released using P-RELEASE, which waits for all queued data to transmit. Two abort services allow forced termination: P-U-ABORT (user-initiated) and P-P-ABORT (provider-initiated). For UDP-based service, retransmission counters and timers ensure the connection request reaches the peer.
sections.plainLanguage: One program sends a request to set up a conversation by saying where it is and where it wants to talk to. They agree on the rules, then talk back and forth. When done, one of them hangs up, or the system breaks the connection if something goes wrong.

sections.title: States and Data Transfer
sections.content: The presentation provider implements a state machine with six states: IDLE (no connection), WAIT1 (connection requested), WAIT2 (connection indicated to user), DATA (connection open), WAIT3 (release requested), and WAIT4 (release indicated to user). Protocol Data Units (PDUs) are exchanged for connect requests, responses, releases, and aborts. The P-DATA service transmits user data (typically remote operations APDUs) in UserData PDUs over an established connection. For TCP-based service, the provider manages TCP connection state; for UDP-based service, it tracks the initiating and responding host addresses and uses session connection identifiers. The serialization module queues outgoing PDUs, applies ASN.1 encoding, and transmits to the network module, which manages the actual transport.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection goes through a series of states: waiting to connect, connected and talking, and waiting to disconnect. Each state says which messages are allowed. Messages get encoded and sent through the pipe.
